title: The Toulmin Model
short: Stephen Toulmin’s model: a claim, the grounds (data) offered for it, and the warrant that links them, with backing, a qualifier and a rebuttal.
trouble: Learners mix up grounds and warrant. The grounds are the specific evidence; the warrant is the general principle, often unstated, that lets the evidence support the claim.

blocks.html: The British philosopher Stephen Toulmin, in The Uses of Argument (1958), described how arguments work in everyday life, the way a case is made in a courtroom, rather than in a logic textbook. His model gives names to the parts of an argument. It builds on patterns of reasoning and on the Logic Ladder’s unstated premises.

head: Part
Answers
Example
rows: Students who start later sleep more and do better in morning classes.
Why does that evidence support the claim?
A school should set its hours to help students learn.
Helping students learn is the purpose of a school.
How sure, how often, how much?
When would the claim not hold?
unless the buses can’t run on the later schedule

blocks.name: wr-toulmin

opts.claim: Our school should start at 8:30 instead of 7:15.
opts.grounds: Students who start later sleep more and do better in morning classes.
opts.warrant: A school should set its hours to help students learn.
opts.backing: Helping students learn is the purpose of a school.
opts.rebuttal: unless the buses can’t run on the later schedule

blocks.cap: Read it as a sentence: grounds, so (probably) claim, since warrant, because backing, unless rebuttal.

blocks.html: An argument offers grounds for a claim; the warrant is the general principle that connects them. Backing supports the warrant, a qualifier says how strong the claim is, and a rebuttal names the exceptions.

Most disagreements aren’t about the evidence; they are about the warrant. Two people can agree that later starts mean more sleep and still disagree about the claim, because one thinks the bus budget matters more. The model shows you where the real disagreement sits, so you can argue about that instead of talking past each other.

blocks.title: Toulmin’s own example
blocks.q: Toulmin’s best-known example, in plain words: Harry was born in Bermuda, so, presumably, Harry is a British subject. Map it.
steps: Grounds: Harry was born in Bermuda.
Claim: Harry is a British subject.
Warrant: a person born in Bermuda will generally be a British subject (as the law stood when Toulmin wrote).
Backing: the laws on nationality that say so.
Qualifier: presumably. Rebuttal: unless, say, both his parents were foreigners or he has since become a citizen of another country.
blocks.a: Grounds → (presumably) claim, since warrant, on account of backing, unless rebuttal.

blocks.title: Map an everyday argument
blocks.q: “The forecast says heavy rain tomorrow, so we should probably move the picnic indoors.” Name the claim, grounds, warrant and qualifier.
steps: Claim (what is argued): we should move the picnic indoors.
Grounds (the evidence): the forecast says heavy rain tomorrow.
Warrant (unstated): forecasts of heavy rain are usually right, and a picnic shouldn’t be held in heavy rain.
blocks.a: Claim: move indoors. Grounds: the forecast. Warrant: heavy-rain forecasts are reliable and picnics need dry weather. Qualifier: probably.

blocks.html: Mixing up grounds and warrant. The grounds are specific: this survey, this forecast, this birth certificate. The warrant is general: a rule or principle that would connect many such facts to many such claims, and it is often left unstated. Check: if the sentence names one particular fact, it is grounds; if it starts “in general” or “any …”, it is likely a warrant.

A note on words: in high school debate, “warrant” often means simply the reason behind a claim (see Building a Case). Toulmin’s warrant is narrower: the general principle that licenses the step from grounds to claim. Both uses are common; say which you mean.
